#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. text.text: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) remains the standard metric for assessing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity, although it does not fully capture the physiological consequences of respiratory events.
Hypoxic burden (HB), which integrates the frequency, depth, and duration of oxygen desaturations, has been proposed as a more comprehensive measure of OSA-related hypoxic stress.
This study compared the prognostic value of HB and AHI for subjective and objective treatment outcomes in patients undergoing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy.
Data from 412 patients with OSA who underwent diagnostic and CPAP-treated polysomnography were analyzed, including 52 patients with available follow-up questionnaires.
HB was calculated using a validated event-based algorithm.
Multivariable regression models were used to predict patientreported outcomes and changes in sleep architecture, adjusted for age, sex and body mass index.
HB consistently demonstrated stronger associations with symptomatic outcomes than AHI.
Models including HB showed improved model fit and explained variance.
HB remained independently associated with lower follow-up fatigue and better sleep quality after adjustment for AHI.
In contrast, AHI was the dominant predictor of objective sleep architecture improvements, including increases in N3 sleep, reductions in N1 sleep, and reductions in arousal index.
HB provided additional independent information only for changes in arousal burden.
These findings suggest that HB and AHI capture complementary dimensions of OSA severity.
While AHI primarily reflects sleep fragmentation and physiological response to CPAP, HB appears more closely related to subjective treatment benefit.
Incorporating HB alongside AHI may improve clinical phenotyping and prediction of treatment response in OSA.
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is one of the most common sleep-related breathing disorders and represents a major public health burden worldwide [1].

text.text: The present study aims to systematically compare AHI and HB as predictors of both subjective and objective treatment outcomes in patients with OSA undergoing CPAP therapy.
Specifically, we examined whether baseline HB provides incremental prognostic value beyond AHI for (1) patientreported outcomes (PROs) and (2) sleep architecture.
Therefore, this study seeks to clarify the potential clinical value of HB for individualized therapy decisions and treatment evaluation in OSA.
This study is based on data from our local clinical sleep dataset.
It was recorded in the sleep laboratory of the Department for Neurology at the University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus in Dresden.

The dataset comprises routine clinical sleep studies from patients, who were referred for the evaluation of sleep disorders, including sleep-related breathing disorders, insomnia, hypersomnia, and movement disorders.
All recordings are standard in-laboratory overnight PSGs.
Recordings were carried out using Alice 5 diagnostic sleep system (Philips Respironics) between 2007 and 2021 and Domino software (SOMNOmedics AG) between 2021 and 2025.

The PSG data includes multimodal physiological signals, such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography, electromyography, respiratory effort, airflow, oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and electrocardiography, enabling comprehensive assessment of sleep architecture and respiratory events.
CPAP therapy recordings were typically conducted one night after the diagnosis night, using a CPAP therapy device.
Sleep stages and respiratory events were scored by trained and experienced PSG technologists and somnologists according to standard clinical criteria from the AASM [16].
text.formatted: Sleep stages and respiratory events were scored by trained and experienced PSG technologists and somnologists according to standard clinical criteria from the AASM <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Diagnoses of sleep disorders were based on the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD) [17].
text.formatted: Diagnoses of sleep disorders were based on the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: PROs were assessed using validated questionnaires, including the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9).
Baseline assessments were obtained at the time of diagnostic PSG night, and follow-up assessments were collected approximately one year later.
PSG recordings from different acquisition systems and file formats were imported and processed using the open-source Sleep Harmonizer framework, which is part of SleePyPhases [18].
text.formatted: PSG recordings from different acquisition systems and file formats were imported and processed using the open-source Sleep Harmonizer framework, which is part of SleePyPhases <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: The Sleep Harmonizer provides a unified interface for loading and harmonizing polysomnographic recordings and annotations across multiple vendor-specific formats, enabling standardized downstream analyses.

For the present analysis, we included all patients diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea who underwent diagnostic night and CPAP therapy nights within three days of each other, both of which were monitored using PSG.
Only cases with available covariate data were included, resulting in a total of 412 cases.
For the analysis of symptomatic outcomes, we additionally only included patients with good CPAP adherence and with available follow-up questionnaire data.
Good CPAP adherence was defined as an average daily use of the CPAP device of at least 4 hours and treatment effectiveness.
This resulted in a total of 52 cases with PROs (see Figure 1).

The hypoxic burden (HB), as defined by Azarbarzin et al. [13], describes the cumulative impact of oxygen desaturations associated with respiratory events.
text.formatted: The hypoxic burden (HB), as defined by Azarbarzin et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, describes the cumulative impact of oxygen desaturations associated with respiratory events.

text.text: It is calculated as the sum of the areas between a pre-event baseline and the oxygen saturation curve, associated with each apnea and hypopnea event.
The HB is designed to integrate both the depth and duration of each desaturation event, thereby providing a more comprehensive picture of hypoxic stress than simple event counts such as AHI.
The algorithm for HB calculation was implemented as follows.
Individual SpO 2 segments associated with manually scored respiratory events are averaged and processed to calculate the search window.
The boundaries of the search window are determined by the two peaks before and after the end of the event of the averaged SpO 2 curve.
The pre-event baseline for each respiratory event is defined as the maximum SpO 2 value within 120 seconds prior to the end of the event.
The area between the baseline and the SpO 2 curve is calculated over the subject-specific search window for each event.
The HB is the cumulative sum of the individual areas, divided by the total sleep time.
We implemented the HB algorithm in Python, based on the MATLAB implementation by Philip de Chazal [19].
text.formatted: We implemented the HB algorithm in Python, based on the MATLAB implementation by Philip de Chazal <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: We adopted it for different sampling rates and optimized the filter function for the averaged SpO 2 signal by using a lowpass FIR filter with cutoff frequency of 0.1 Hz to smooth the signal.
Our implementation can be found under the MIT License on GitLab, see https://gitlab.com/sleep-is-all-you-need/hypoxic-burden.
text.formatted: Our implementation can be found under the MIT License on GitLab, see <ref type="url" target="https://gitlab.com/sleep-is-all-you-need/hypoxic-burden">https://gitlab.com/sleep-is- all-you-need/hypoxic-burden</ref>.

text.text: We evaluated and tested our HB implementation thoroughly on the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) dataset [21], comprising nearly 5,800 polysomnographic recordings.
text.formatted: We evaluated and tested our HB implementation thoroughly on the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, comprising nearly 5,800 polysomnographic recordings.

text.text: The dataset was provided by the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR) [22].

text.text: The implemented HB algorithm showed excellent agreement with the reference implementation in MATLAB by Philip de Chazal.
This was demonstrated by near-perfect Pearson correlation (r > 0.999) and minimal systematic bias (bias = -1.15 %min/h).
text.formatted: This was demonstrated by near-perfect Pearson correlation (r > 0.999) and minimal systematic bias (bias = -1.15 %min/h).

text.text: However, the definition and selection of the respiratory events used as input for the algorithm have a substantial impact on the resulting HB values.
We observed that the annotated apnea and hypopnea events in the SHHS polysomnography data do not directly correspond to the events used to calculate the specified AHI value in the SHHS dataset files.
Although there are quite a few different AHI definitions, the number of annotated respiratory events exceeds the values included in all of these definitions.
This is most likely because all scored apnea and hypopneas events are listed in the annotations, and even basic criteria for AHI calculation are applied afterwards.
For instance, if an apnea was scored during a wake epoch, it would still be listed in the respiratory event list but not considered in any AHI calculation.
While this is conclusive in itself, it creates the additional task of event selection for event-based algorithms.
Therefore, a harmonized event selection was required to ensure consistency between calculation of HB and AHI.
We replicated the AHI according to the definition "ahi_a0h3" from the SHHS dataset.
The AHI was defined as the total number of apneas and hypopneas divided by the total sleep time in hours.
For apneas, the criteria were a ≥ 90 % drop in airflow for ≥ 10 seconds without oxygen desaturation threshold and with or without arousals.
For hypopneas, the criteria were a ≥ 30 % drop in airflow for ≥ 10 seconds, as well as a ≥ 3 % oxygen desaturation from a pre-event baseline with or without arousals.
Oxygen desaturation was computed relative to a pre-event baseline, defined as the maximum of a 120-second window preceding event onset.
Additionally, the calculation only includes apneas and hypopneas that began during sleep.
After automatically applying these filtering criteria to the annotated respiratory events, the resulting AHI values showed strong agreement with the SHHS reference values.

The comparison between the implemented AHI and the ahi_a0h3 reference demonstrated a very high correlation (Pearson r = 0.981, p < 0.001), with a small systematic bias of -0.50 events/h, indicating a slight underestimation relative to the reference method, most likely due to slight implementation differences of the event selection rules.
text.formatted: The comparison between the implemented AHI and the ahi_a0h3 reference demonstrated a very high correlation (Pearson r = 0.981, p < 0.001), with a small systematic bias of -0.50 events/h, indicating a slight underestimation relative to the reference method, most likely due to slight implementation differences of the event selection rules.

text.text: Using the same respiratory event definitions, HB and AHI were calculated for our local clinical dataset.

Multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to evaluate the incremental prognostic value of HB beyond the AHI in predicting symptomatic and physiological responses to CPAP treatment in patients with OSA.
The two outcome domains, PROs and PSG-derived outcomes, were analyzed.
PROs included daytime sleepiness (ESS), fatigue (FSS), sleep quality (PSQI), and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9).
For these analyses, follow-up questionnaire scores obtained approximately one year after diagnostic night served as dependent variables while adjusting for baseline questionnaire scores.
PSG-derived outcomes included N3 sleep (%), N1 sleep (%), REM latency, and arousal index.

For PSG-derived outcomes, treatment effects were quantified as the difference between the CPAP therapy night and the diagnostic night: Model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R²), reflecting explained variance, and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), which assesses model fit while penalizing model complexity.
Comparisons across Models A, B, and AB were used to determine the relative predictive value of AHI and HB.

The inclusion of both predictors in Model AB enabled evaluation of whether HB contributed unique explanatory information after accounting for AHI, while also allowing assessment of the independent associations of each OSA severity metric with treatment outcomes.
Model assumptions were assessed using residual diagnostics, including tests for normality (Omnibus and Jarque-Bera tests).
Due to deviations from normality in several models, robust standard errors (HC1) were calculated as sensitivity analyses.
Results were considered robust if statistical significance remained consistent.
Statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
text.formatted: Statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text.text: In the AHI-only models (Model A), higher AHI at diagnostic night was associated with lower follow-up ESS scores (β = -0.075, p = 0.003), whereas no significant associations were observed for fatigue (FSS), sleep quality (PSQI), or depressive symptoms (PHQ-9).

In contrast, higher HB at diagnostic night was significantly associated with lower follow-up symptom burden across all investigated PROs in the HBonly models (Model B), including ESS (β = -0.017, p = 0.001), FSS (β = -0.026, p = 0.023), PSQI (β = -0.009, p = 0.023), and PHQ-9 (β = -0.007, p = 0.041).
When both metrics were entered simultaneously (Model AB), associations between AHI and followup symptom burden were no longer statistically significant.

In contrast, HB remained independently associated with lower follow-up fatigue (β = -0.074, p = 0.015) and better sleep quality (β = -0.026, p = 0.018), whereas associations with daytime sleepiness and depressive symptoms were attenuated and no longer significant after adjustment for AHI.
Overall, models including HB demonstrated superior explanatory performance compared with models including AHI alone.

text.text: Shown are the independent effects of apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and hypoxic burden (HB) at diagnostic night, each adjusted for age, sex, and BMI.
In this study, we assessed the incremental value of HB for OSA treatment.
Therefore, we compared the prognostic value of HB with AHI for both PROs and PSG-derived parameters.

As the main finding, HB consistently provided clinically relevant information beyond AHI for symptomatic outcomes, whereas AHI remained more strongly related to changes in sleep architecture as a response to CPAP therapy.
These results suggest that AHI and HB reflect complementary pathophysiological dimensions of OSA.
Across multiple PROs, including daytime sleepiness, fatigue, sleep quality, and depressive symptoms, HB emerged as the more consistent independent predictor of follow-up symptom burden than AHI.
Models including HB generally demonstrated better fit than models including AHI alone, and associations between AHI and symptomatic outcomes disappeared after adjustment for HB.
This pattern indicates that the apparent relationship between AHI and symptom improvement is largely driven by the hypoxic component of respiratory events rather than event frequency itself.
Baseline questionnaire scores were the strongest predictors of follow-up values, resulting in overall high explained variance (R² values 0.565-0.843).
Adding HB to the models consistently improved model fit, as reflected by higher R² and lower AIC values compared with models including AHI alone.
From a clinical perspective, these findings support the concept that OSA severity and expected treatment benefits should not be assessed solely by the number of respiratory events.
While AHI quantifies event frequency, it does not adequately capture the physiological burden imposed by repeated oxygen desaturations.
HB may therefore represent the clinically more relevant dimension of subjective disease severity, particularly with regard to daytime functioning and treatment-related symptom improvement.
This was particularly evident for fatigue and sleep quality, where higher baseline HB was associated with lower residual symptom burden at follow-up.
These findings suggest that patients with greater nocturnal hypoxic stress showed lower residual symptom burden following CPAP therapy after adjustment for baseline symptom severity.
This suggests that HB may identify patients more likely to experience favorable symptomatic response to CPAP.

Our findings support the clinical relevance of HB as a marker of disease severity and treatment response, as HB is a stronger predictor of symptomatic outcomes, such as daytime sleepiness and fatigue.
This aligns with prior evidence from pediatric populations, where HB was shown to correlate more closely with symptom burden than the AHI [23].
text.formatted: This aligns with prior evidence from pediatric populations, where HB was shown to correlate more closely with symptom burden than the AHI <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: HB was associated with sleep architecture changes in single-predictor models.
However, after adjustment for AHI, most associations disappeared, indicating that these effects were largely shared with respiratory event frequency.
AHI remained the dominant predictor of sleep architecture response, particularly increases in N3 sleep, reductions in N1 sleep, shorter REM latency, and lower arousal burden.
In contrast, HB provided additional information only for changes in arousal burden.

The consistent pattern of best R² for Model AB, but best AIC for Model A reflects, that the improvements in sleep architecture are best explained (R² ) by the combination of AHI and HB, but simplest explained (AIC) by just AHI.
These findings suggest that respiratory event frequency primarily reflects the mechanical burden of repetitive airway obstruction and associated sleep fragmentation.
Patients with higher AHI may therefore show greater immediate normalization of sleep continuity once obstructive events are eliminated during CPAP.
By comparison, HB is less relevant to predict these acute changes in sleep structure.
Additionally, regression models were carried out for sleep microstructure parameters such as the spindle index and delta power.
However, no statistically significant results could be obtained for either AHI or HB, and the model performance was very poor for these outcomes.
Therefore, they were not reported in detail in this article.
Taken together, our results indicate that AHI and HB should not be viewed as competing metrics, but rather as complementary measures.

By that interpretation, AHI characterizes fragmentation-related sleep disruption, whereas HB represents the physiological consequences of intermittent hypoxemia and their relationship to subjective clinical symptoms.
Current clinical classification of OSA relies predominantly on AHI thresholds.
However, patients with similar AHI values often differ substantially in symptom burden, cardiovascular risk, and treatment response [11], [13].
text.formatted: However, patients with similar AHI values often differ substantially in symptom burden, cardiovascular risk, and treatment response <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings add to the growing evidence that metrics incorporating hypoxic stress may improve phenotyping and risk stratification.
HB showed independent incremental value in multivariable models and may help identify patients more likely to benefit symptomatically from CPAP therapy.
This could be particularly relevant for individuals with inconsistent clinical presentations, such as a high symptom burden despite a moderate AHI, or limited symptoms despite a severe AHI.
Accordingly, future approaches to OSA assessment may benefit from integrating both event frequency and hypoxic burden rather than relying on AHI alone.
Several limitations should be considered.
Firstly, the number of available follow-up questionnaires was comparatively small, resulting in a small sample size for PRO analyses (n = 52), which limits statistical power and generalizability.
Therefore, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and require replication in larger and more diverse cohorts.
In contrast, analyses of PSG-derived outcomes were conducted in a substantially larger cohort (n = 412).
One limitation relates to the scoring of hypopneas.
According to the AASM criteria, hypopneas may be defined either by a ≥ 3 % oxygen desaturation or by an associated arousal.
In the present study, hypopneas were scored based on the oxygen desaturation criterion only, whereas arousal-related hypopneas without accompanying desaturation were not included.
This may have led to an underestimation of respiratory events compared with full AASM scoring.
However, identical apnea and hypopnea events were used for the calculation of both AHI and HB, ensuring internal methodological consistency across metrics.
Regarding the HB calculation, no universally accepted standard algorithm currently exists.
Different computational approaches have been proposed, limiting comparability across studies and currently restricting routine clinical implementation [10], [12].
text.formatted: Different computational approaches have been proposed, limiting comparability across studies and currently restricting routine clinical implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, clinically meaningful threshold values for HB have not yet been clearly defined, which currently constrains direct translation into treatment algorithms or severity classification.
Existing HB algorithms may incompletely capture certain respiratory event characteristics, particularly prolonged events or complex desaturation patterns.

Although the algorithm is designed to capture the depth and duration of desaturations, it calculates a patient-specific search window that averages the length of the desaturations and defines a uniform duration for each patient.
Consequently, longer events are not fully captured.
In addition, HB depends on accurate scoring of respiratory events and therefore remains influenced by manual event annotation.
In contrast, alternative approaches such as time under 90 % oxygen saturation (T90) or accumulated desaturation area metrics quantify nocturnal hypoxemia directly from the oximetry signal.
An ideal metric would capture hypoxic stress independently of manually annotated respiratory events.
Finally, HB is highly correlated with AHI, which may complicate simultaneous modeling and limit interpretability in multivariable analyses due to collinearity.

HB improved prediction of several symptomatic outcomes as a response to CPAP treatment, particularly fatigue and sleep quality, whereas AHI remained the dominant predictor of short-term sleep architecture changes.
These findings support the interpretation that respiratory event frequency and hypoxic burden capture distinct but complementary aspects of OSA severity.
Incorporating HB alongside AHI may improve clinical phenotyping and better explain heterogeneity in treatment response.
